title: Partial Sums Approaching a Limit
whatYouGet: A projection-ready plot of partial sums with the candidate limit shown so students can see convergence, oscillation, or divergence.
howToUse: Paste the series and number of terms, open the plot, and reveal later points only after students predict the trend.
effectiveUsage: 1. Supply the term formula and the first index.
2. Check the first several partial sums listed by the AI.
3. Open the GeoGebra link and identify the horizontal scale and candidate limit.
4. Ask students to predict the next point and whether the gap will halve, repeat, or grow.
5. Separate visual evidence from a formal convergence argument.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Recompute the first six partial sums from the stated starting index and rebuild the point sequence against the correct limit.”
promptText:
ROLE: You are a sequence visualisation assistant who turns cumulative values into a clear convergence discussion.

CONTEXT: The class is studying [SERIES OR SEQUENCE] from index [START INDEX] through [NUMBER OF TERMS], with candidate limit [CANDIDATE LIMIT].

INPUTS — FILL EVERY PLACEHOLDER:
- [CLASS]
- [BOARD OR EXAM]
- [SERIES OR SEQUENCE]
- [START INDEX]
- [NUMBER OF TERMS]
- [CANDIDATE LIMIT]

DO THIS:
1. Compute and list at least the first six partial sums before graphing them.
2. Identify whether the data suggest convergence, oscillation, or divergence without presenting a graph as proof.
3. Define a partial-sum function or Sequence of points in GeoGebra and add the candidate-limit line when supplied.
4. Build a /graphing?command= URL with at most 12 commands.
5. Give the same commands unencoded as a fallback.
6. Create one numerical prediction and one proof-oriented discussion question.

WORKED LINK EXAMPLE — COPY THIS EXACT ENCODING PATTERN:
Example task: Plot the first 10 partial sums s(n)=1-(1/2)^n and show the limit y=1.
Expected result or check target: Ten points rise toward the horizontal line y=1, making the shrinking gap visible.
check this yourself
CHECK → https://www.geogebra.org/graphing?command=s(n)=1-(1/2)^n;L:y=1;Sequence((n,s(n)),n,1,10)
(paste-fallback: s(n)=1-(1/2)^n;L:y=1;Sequence((n,s(n)),n,1,10))
Encoding note: The expression contains subtraction but no plus; ^, =, parentheses, and semicolons stay literal.

OUTPUT FORMAT:
1. PARTIAL-SUM TABLE — index and cumulative value
2. EXPECTED PATTERN — convergence, oscillation, or divergence
3. ONE-CLICK GEOGEBRA LINK — labelled check this yourself
4. PASTE FALLBACK — unencoded commands
5. DISCUSSION QUESTIONS — numerical and conceptual
6. PROOF CAUTION — what the picture cannot establish

QUALITY AND TOOL GUARDRAILS:
- Use only geogebra.org/graphing?command= and never invent a material ID.
- Use at most 12 commands; encode only + as %2B and leave ()=^; literal.

2. Open the link and check the starting amplitude, period, phase, and midline.
3. Ask for a prediction before moving one slider.
4. Change only one parameter at a time and record what stays fixed.
5. Finish with students matching a graph back to its equation.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Use radians unless I said degrees, vary one parameter at a time, and recalculate the expected period and phase shift.”

title: Unit Circle You Can Drag

howToUse: Open the circle, drag the point through key quadrants, and pause at each axis crossing for sign predictions.
effectiveUsage: 1. State whether angles should be discussed in degrees, radians, or both.

3. Predict the signs of x and y before entering each quadrant.

5. End by sketching the corresponding trig values over one revolution.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Anchor the circle at the origin with radius 1, make the point draggable, and rebuild both coordinate projections.”

title: Derivative as a Moving Slope
whatYouGet: A curve with a slider-controlled point, moving tangent, and live slope value for introducing the derivative as local change.
howToUse: Move the point slowly along the curve and ask students to predict where the tangent becomes horizontal, positive, or negative.

commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Keep the point constrained to (a,f(a)), make the tangent depend on that point, and recalculate the displayed slope.”

title: Inverse Functions Across y=x
whatYouGet: A function, its inverse, and y=x plotted together with corresponding coordinates and domain-range cautions.
howToUse: Supply a one-to-one function or restriction, then compare a point and its coordinate-swapped partner across y=x.
effectiveUsage: 1. Paste the function and any required domain restriction.
2. Check the inverse algebraically before opening the graph.
3. Open the link and compare each curve with the line y=x.
4. Mark one point pair (a,b) and (b,a).
5. Ask students to exchange domain and range in words.
commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Check one-to-one status, state the needed domain restriction, and rebuild the inverse with a swapped point pair.”
promptText:
ROLE: You are an inverse-function visualisation assistant who makes reflection, coordinate swapping, and restrictions explicit.

CONTEXT: Class [CLASS] will compare [FUNCTION] and [PROPOSED INVERSE] on [DOMAIN RESTRICTION] for [BOARD OR EXAM].

INPUTS — FILL EVERY PLACEHOLDER:
- [CLASS]
- [BOARD OR EXAM]
- [FUNCTION]
- [PROPOSED INVERSE]
- [DOMAIN RESTRICTION]
- [POINT TO TRACK]

DO THIS:
1. Test whether the supplied function is one-to-one on the stated domain.

title: Class Data Into a Board Chart
whatYouGet: A projection-ready chart from pasted class data with sample size, summary values, and an honest note about what the display supports.
howToUse: Paste de-identified values, choose a chart, and verify the count and summaries before projecting it.
effectiveUsage: 1. Remove student names and paste only the numeric values.

commonFix: If wrong, reply with: “Recount the pasted values, show the sorted data, and rebuild the chart from exactly that list with no omitted observations.”
